title: Known Completely by God
subtitle: Omniscience, prayer, and the searching love of God
summary: Psalm 139 approaches divine knowledge through prayer rather than an abstract inventory of information. Learn to distinguish the psalm’s witness from later philosophical models.

scripture.text: LORD, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but behold, LORD, you know it altogether.
scripture.context: Read the whole of Psalm 139, including its difficult verses 19–22 and final request for examination in verses 23–24. The psalm moves through divine knowledge, presence, creation, opposition to wickedness, and prayer.

objectives: Describe divine knowledge as Psalm 139 presents it.
Recognize the difference between poetic testimony and a philosophical model.
Connect being known by God with honest prayer and responsibility.
essentialQuestions: How does the psalm’s final prayer shape its opening confession?
What does complete knowledge mean for honesty?
Which questions about knowledge and freedom remain beyond this passage?

sections.title: Knowledge spoken as prayer
paragraphs: Omniscience is a theological term for God’s complete knowledge. Psalm 139 begins with an address to the LORD, moving from daily actions to thoughts and unspoken words. Its language is personal: the speaker is searched and known. The psalm does not merely argue that God possesses more information than humans. It depicts a life lived before a knowledge the speaker cannot escape or comprehend.

The confession ends with a request to be searched, tried, and led. That ending matters. If God already knows, prayer is not supplying missing information. It is an act of truthful relation, asking that one’s way be brought into the light. A group can therefore study the attribute without turning it into a technique for guessing other people’s motives. Being known by God does not make a human leader all-knowing.

sections.title: Poetry, presence, and embodied life
paragraphs: The psalm’s journeys to height, depth, distant sea, and darkness dramatize the impossibility of leaving God’s presence. Its account of formation in the womb likewise places the speaker’s embodied history before God. These images belong to Hebrew poetry as rendered by the WEB. They are not a modern anatomical account or a literal itinerary of the universe.

Read the difficult part as well as the comforting part. Verses 19–22 contain fierce opposition to the wicked. A teacher should neither delete them nor immediately turn them into a command for hostility toward a neighbor. The closing appeal for God to examine the speaker also invites scrutiny of the speaker’s own heart. This lesson offers that literary connection as an interpretation open to pastoral discussion.

sections.title: The attribute and the limits of a model
paragraphs: First John 3:19–20 speaks of God as greater than the heart and knowing all things. Its surrounding concern is confidence before God expressed in practical love. That setting helps prevent an account of divine knowledge from becoming only a source of terror. The chapter calls readers to action and truth while directing them beyond their own condemning heart.

The Baptist Faith and Message explicitly describes God’s knowledge as extending to past, present, future, and future decisions. Westminster gives a Reformed account of God’s decree alongside creaturely agency. These statements demonstrate how traditions formulate the question; they do not make a short psalm a complete philosophical treatise. Debates about timelessness, providence, and freedom require definitions and additional sources.

sections.title: A truthful life before God
paragraphs: A pastoral response may begin with honest prayer: gratitude for being seen, confession of what is concealed, or lament over what feels unbearable. The psalm provides language for this response without giving a leader permission to demand every private detail from a congregant. God’s knowledge and human access to another person’s story are different matters.

For study, place the psalm’s opening and closing side by side. Note what God knows and what the speaker requests. Then name one practice of integrity that follows: acknowledging a mistake, seeking appropriate help, or stopping an effort to manage appearances. This is an application drawn from the prayer, not an additional verse or a guarantee of immediate emotional relief.

sections.title: A distinction worth preserving
paragraphs: A leader can invite honest prayer while respecting a person’s privacy. “God knows” is not equivalent to “the group must know.” This distinction matters when a discussion concerns painful memories or sensitive relationships. The final prayer of Psalm 139 is addressed to God; it should not be turned into a demand for public disclosure. Encourage appropriate support, truthful self-examination, and consent in the way the group listens.

languageNote.meaning: A doctrinal label for the completeness of divine knowledge.
languageNote.caution: The term is a later theological label, not the original-language wording of Psalm 139. The lesson does not derive a philosophical system from an alleged Hebrew root.

consensus: The profile affirms God’s complete knowledge. Psalm 139 and 1 John 3 provide biblical witness; the precise relation between knowledge, time, and creaturely freedom calls for additional theological explanation.
disputed: Christian accounts of providence, foreknowledge, and freedom vary. Statements that God “learns” or that prayer “changes God’s knowledge” need explicit definitions and confessional review rather than casual acceptance or dismissal.
application: Pray the opening and closing of Psalm 139 with attention to their connection.
Practice truthful confession without claiming access to another person’s hidden motives.
reflection: What difference does being known make to my prayer?
Where am I trying to protect an appearance rather than tell the truth?
discussion: Why should the difficult verses remain in a lesson about this psalm?
What is the difference between God’s knowledge and a leader’s claim to know another person?

quiz.question: What does Psalm 139 ask in its conclusion?
options: That God search and lead the speaker
That every philosophical dispute be resolved
quiz.explanation: Verses 23–24 ask God to search, examine, and lead the speaker.

quiz.question: What is omniscience here?
options: A Hebrew personal name in Psalm 139
A later theological label for divine knowledge
A license to infer others’ motives
quiz.explanation: The doctrinal label summarizes a topic; it is not the psalm’s original-language wording.
